title: CI Fundamentals
summary: Continuous integration is the discipline of merging small changes often and proving them automatically. Learn why it beats the old branch-and-integrate model, and how a fast, trusted pipeline becomes the team's shared nervous system.

slides.markdown:
**Continuous Integration (CI)** means every developer merges their changes into a shared branch frequently — at least daily — and a machine automatically builds and tests that merge, every time, with no human deciding whether to bother.

The practice sounds almost too simple to name. It earns the name because of what it replaces: teams that let branches diverge for weeks and only discover they conflict, or break each other's code, at integration time — usually right before a release, when there's the least time to fix it.

CI's real product isn't the pipeline. It's **information, fast**: within minutes of a change, everyone knows whether the codebase still works. Everything else in this group — deployment, flags, release process — assumes that signal exists and is trustworthy.

slides.subTitle: Merge often, verify automatically
slides.markdown:
Two commitments make something CI, not just "we have a build script":

- **Merge often.** Changes land on the shared branch in small, frequent increments — hours or a day of work, not weeks. Small diffs are easier to review, easier to test, and cheap to revert.
- **Verify automatically, on every merge.** No one has to remember to run the tests, and no one can skip it because they're confident. The machine builds and tests every single change, unconditionally.

Neither commitment alone is CI. A team that merges constantly but never runs automated tests just breaks things faster. A team with a great test suite that only runs it before a release has CI's tooling without its practice — they've reinvented the integration-hell schedule, just with better instrumentation once it happens.

slides.subTitle: "It works on my machine"
slides.markdown:
Before CI was standard practice, teams commonly worked in long-lived feature branches for weeks, then tried to merge them all near a release date. This was called **integration hell** for a reason: dozens of branches, each individually fine, colliding with each other in ways no single developer could predict.

The other half of the pre-CI world was environment drift. A change would pass on a developer's laptop — the right compiler version, a stale dependency, a config file only they had — and fail everywhere else. "Works on my machine" became the default punchline because there was no shared, automatic arbiter of truth.

CI fixes both at once: merging small and often shrinks each individual integration to something trivial, and running it in a clean, identical environment every time removes the laptop as a variable.

Stripped to its essence, CI is a loop with four steps that runs on every push:

1. A developer **pushes** a commit (usually as part of a pull request).
2. A CI server **builds** the code in a clean environment.
3. The build is **tested** — unit tests at minimum, often more.
4. The result is **reported back** to the pull request as a pass/fail status, visible to reviewers and the author.

The loop is deliberately synchronous with the PR: the status shows up where the decision to merge is being made, not in a separate dashboard someone has to remember to check. That placement is what turns a test suite into a gate rather than a suggestion.

slides.sectionTitle: The feedback loop is the whole point
slides.subTitle: Fast fail beats slow fail
slides.markdown:
CI's value scales inversely with how long it takes to tell you something is wrong. A failure caught in 3 minutes costs you a context switch. The same failure caught in 3 days costs you re-remembering the change, re-establishing the mental state, and often untangling it from three other changes that landed on top of it since.

This is why CI practitioners obsess over pipeline speed almost as much as correctness. A 90-second pipeline gets run and trusted; a 45-minute one gets batched around — developers stack up several PRs before running it, which quietly recreates integration hell in miniature.

The practical target most teams aim for: keep the **required**, merge-blocking checks under 10 minutes, and push anything slower (full end-to-end suites, performance tests) to run asynchronously after merge, not before it.

slides.sectionTitle: Build status as a merge gate
slides.subTitle: Required checks, branch protection
slides.markdown:
A CI result only changes behavior if it's enforced. Most hosting platforms let you configure **branch protection** on the shared branch: a set of **required checks** that must pass before the merge button is even clickable, regardless of what a reviewer thinks.

This matters because it removes a human failure mode — a reviewer approving code they didn't fully re-verify, trusting that "tests probably pass." With a required check, that trust isn't needed; the platform simply refuses the merge until CI reports green.

Well-configured branch protection typically requires: the build/test check, at least one code-review approval, and an up-to-date branch (rebased or merged with the latest shared branch) before merging — the last one catches the case where your change was fine against last week's main but not against what landed an hour ago.

Most CI configs boil down to a short list of stages, declared as code and versioned alongside the app. A typical shape:

```yaml
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  build-and-test:
    steps:
      - checkout
      - run: npm ci            # install, exact locked versions
      - run: npm run build     # compile / bundle
      - run: npm test          # unit + integration tests
      - run: npm run lint      # static checks, style
```

Each stage exists to fail fast on a specific class of problem: `install` catches a broken or unpinned dependency before anything else runs, `build` catches compile-time errors, `test` catches behavioral regressions, and `lint` catches the style and static-analysis issues that are cheap to check but expensive to review manually.

Order matters for speed: put the cheapest, most-likely-to-fail stage first so a broken change fails in seconds, not after a ten-minute build.

The shared branch (commonly `main`) is meant to be **always green and always deployable** — any commit on it, at any time, could in principle be shipped. This is the property CI exists to protect, and it's also the foundation **trunk-based development** builds on: developers integrate directly into a single shared trunk in small increments, rather than living in long branches, precisely because CI makes that safe.

The discipline this demands is subtle: if your change might break main, it shouldn't merge — which pushes risky, half-finished work behind a **feature flag** (covered in this group's flags topic) rather than a long-lived branch. The branch stays short-lived; the incomplete feature stays invisible, not unmerged.

A team that treats "main is green" as a hard invariant, not an aspiration, gets a large compounding benefit: anyone can deploy from main at any moment with confidence, which is what makes fast, frequent releases possible at all.

slides.sectionTitle: Shaping the suite for CI speed
slides.subTitle: Not every test belongs in the merge-blocking path
slides.markdown:
A common trap: teams equate "more tests in CI" with "safer," and pile every test — including slow end-to-end browser suites and full integration tests against real infrastructure — into the required, merge-blocking check. Pipeline time climbs past 30–40 minutes, and the fast-feedback benefit of CI quietly dies.

The fix is tiering, roughly following the **test pyramid**: a large base of fast unit tests runs on every push and blocks merge; a smaller layer of integration tests runs the same way if it's fast enough; and the slowest suites — full end-to-end, cross-service, load tests — run **after** merge, on a schedule, or on a nightly build, reporting failures without blocking the developer who's waiting to ship.

This isn't lowering the bar. It moves the bar to where it does the most good: nothing merges without unit-level proof, and the expensive proof still runs — just not in the critical path of every single commit.

The single most corrosive CI failure mode isn't a slow pipeline — it's a **red main that stays red**. One flaky test fails intermittently, someone shrugs and merges anyway because "it's probably not my change," and within a week the team has quietly retrained itself to treat CI failures as noise.

Once that happens, CI stops doing its job entirely: a real regression hides inside the pile of tolerated red, and nobody notices until it reaches production. The pipeline is still running — it just isn't being *believed*.

The recovery discipline has to be near-immediate: a broken main gets fixed or the breaking commit gets reverted within minutes, not hours, and it's treated as the team's top priority, not the responsible engineer's private problem. Teams that hold this line strictly find CI stays trustworthy indefinitely; teams that let it slip even once tend to need a painful, deliberate reset to earn the trust back.

slides.sectionTitle: CI is a team discipline, not a tool
slides.markdown:
It's tempting to think of CI as infrastructure you buy or configure once. In practice, the pipeline is the easy part; the discipline around it is what determines whether it works.

Teams that get real value from CI tend to share a few unwritten rules: **you broke it, you own the fix** — immediately, not at the end of the sprint; **no merging around red** — a failing required check is not a suggestion; and **the pipeline itself gets maintained** — someone owns pruning flaky tests and watching pipeline duration creep, the same way someone owns the codebase's architecture.

Without that ownership, CI degrades exactly the way any unmaintained system does: flaky tests accumulate, duration creeps up, and the team's tolerance for "just re-run it" grows until the signal is gone. The tooling questions in the rest of this group — pipeline design, caching, scaling — only pay off on top of that baseline discipline.
